title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: Accounting net profit is an opinion formed by management; cash in the bank is an audited fact of reality.
epigraph.author: Forensic accounting maxim

web_blocks.text: A forensic examination of Kody Technolab’s multi-year financial statements reveals a profound dichotomy between accounting earnings and structural cash generation. Over the historical reporting window from FY22 through FY26 and trailing-twelve-month (TTM) period through September 2026, consolidated revenue surged from ₹11.20 crore to ₹80.00 crore, and further to ₹111.00 crore TTM. Operating profit expanded from ₹3.10 crore to ₹24.00 crore in FY26 and ₹26.00 crore TTM, with reported operating profit margins (OPM) oscillating between 30% and 35% before moderating to 23% in recent periods. On paper, this resembles a textbook growth compounding trajectory. However, beneath the headline P&L lies extreme working capital absorption, deeply negative free cash flows, elevated reliance on non-operating other income, and serial balance sheet dilution. [1][6]

web_blocks.caption: Kody Technolab multi-year financial & cash conversion forensics (₹ crore, audited consolidated figures)
rows: Strong top-line expansion (+118% over 2 years) driven by robotics pivot.
OPM contracted from 35% in FY25 to 30% in FY26 and 23% TTM as hardware BOM mix grew.
Sharp escalation: other income represents 27% of FY26 PBT and 31% of TTM PBT. (Alert)
Net profit flatlined despite revenue growth; ₹7 Cr of FY26 PAT came from other income.
Weak cash conversion: CFO/EBITDA of 50%, heavily impaired by trade receivables.
Heavy investing outflows for Gandhinagar assembly plant, demo fleet, and tooling.
Deeply negative free cash flow; business has incinerated cash throughout the expansion.
Relentless deterioration: over 6 months of sales locked in uncollected customer invoices.
Severe balance sheet stretch: working capital exploded more than three-fold in FY26.
Promoter stake diluted by 4.19% via non-promoter warrants and preferential allotments.
web_blocks.takeaway: Accounting PAT of ₹17 Cr is decoupled from cash reality: FY26 generated -₹53 Cr in Free Cash Flow and debtor days stretched to 192 days, requiring serial equity dilution. [1][6][7]

web_blocks.caption: Multi-year audited consolidated Profit & Loss statement from Screener fundamentals ledger
web_blocks.takeaway: Audited consolidated sales rose from ₹72 Cr in FY25 to ₹80 Cr in FY26 and ₹111 Cr TTM, while operating margins moderated from 35% to 23% and other income expanded to ₹9 Cr. [1]

web_blocks.text: The first forensic warning flag centers on Earnings Quality and Non-Operating Income Reliance. In FY25, other income was a negligible ₹1.00 crore against profit before tax of ₹24.00 crore (4.2% of PBT). In FY26, other income spiked seven-fold to ₹7.00 crore against PBT of ₹26.00 crore, accounting for 26.9% of pre-tax earnings and over 41% of net profit (₹17.00 crore). On a trailing-twelve-month basis, other income expanded further to ₹9.00 crore against PBT of ₹29.00 crore (31.0% of PBT). This non-operating income originates from treasury management of unutilized preferential issue proceeds, fixed deposit interest, and fair-value revaluation gains. An analyst must recognize that core operating manufacturing and software earnings have effectively flatlined over the past eighteen months. Reported bottom-line stability was heavily manufactured by treasury returns. [1][6]

web_blocks.caption: Audited consolidated Balance Sheet evolution from Screener fundamentals ledger
web_blocks.takeaway: Total balance sheet footings expanded from ₹112 Cr in Mar 2025 to ₹266 Cr in Mar 2026 and ₹298 Cr in Sep 2026, driven by reserve accretion from preferential warrants and fixed asset additions. [1]

web_blocks.text: The second forensic warning flag is the severe structural deterioration of Working Capital and Trade Receivables. As documented in the ratios ledger, trade debtor days expanded from 103 days at the time of the IPO to 163 days in FY24, 177 days in FY25, and reached 192 days in FY26. Concurrently, net working capital days exploded from 62 days in FY25 to 197 days in FY26. On a consolidated balance sheet of ₹298 crore in September 2026, other assets (principally trade receivables, unbilled project assets, and vendor capital advances) stood at ₹177 crore. This represents nearly 60% of total company assets. In an industrial equipment company, high debtor days signal either aggressive channel stuffing, uncollected overseas distributor bills, or disputes over installation milestones. [1][6]

web_blocks.caption: Audited consolidated Cash Flow forensics from Screener fundamentals ledger
web_blocks.takeaway: Operating cash flow was ₹10 Cr in FY25 and ₹12 Cr in FY26, heavily impaired by working capital outflows, while investing cash outflows reached ₹51 Cr and ₹86 Cr, generating severe cash deficits. [1]

web_blocks.text: The third forensic dimension is Cash Flow Disconnection and Capital Destruction. While cumulative reported net profit across FY25 and FY26 totaled ₹35.00 crore, cumulative operating cash flow was only ₹22.00 crore. After accounting for ₹116.00 crore in cash capital expenditures and investing outflows over the two-year period, cumulative free cash flow was negative ₹94.00 crore (negative ₹41.00 crore in FY25 and negative ₹53.00 crore in FY26). The business has run an immense structural cash deficit throughout its growth phase. Financing cash flows—comprising ₹37.00 crore in FY25 and ₹113.00 crore in FY26—bridged this chasm through equity dilution and borrowings rather than operating self-funding. [1][6]

web_blocks.caption: Multi-year audited operational and capital efficiency ratios from Screener fundamentals ledger
web_blocks.takeaway: ROCE stood at 18% in FY26 while ROE moderated to 11.4%; debtor days of 192 days and working capital days of 197 days confirm structural capital absorption. [1]

web_blocks.text: The fourth forensic dimension is Share Capital Dilution and Per-Share Comparability. The company's balance sheet reserves expanded from ₹66 crore in March 2025 to ₹201 crore in March 2026. Also, further to ₹215 crore by September 2026, reflecting continuous equity expansion via preferential warrants. In 2026, the NSE listed an additional 13.88 lakh equity shares arising from warrant conversions. As a result, promoter shareholding decreased from 73.01% across 2023–2025 down to 69.49% in September 2026 and 68.82% by October 2026. While short-term earnings per share (EPS) appears resilient at ₹12.20 TTM, it is being diluted by a steadily expanding share count and inflated by non-operating treasury income. [1][6][7]

In forensic synthesis, Kody Technolab's financial reality does not reflect a self-sustaining technology compounder. Instead, it reflects an emerging, capital-hungry hardware growth story whose operating cash generation is swamped by trade debtor lockup and assembly capex. Return on capital employed (ROCE) of 17.7% and return on equity (ROE) of 11.4% remain respectable only because balance sheet equity is buoyed by treasury cash reserves. Until operating cash flows turn decisively positive and free cash flow deficits reverse, the quality of earnings must be underwritten with intense institutional skepticism. [1][6]

book_paragraphs: Now let you and I leave the factory floor and sit down with Kody's audited financial ledgers. This is where an analyst must be completely unemotional. Management can tell whatever story they like in television interviews, but the balance sheet and the cash flow statement are the unsparing truth. When you look at Kody's multi-year numbers, what do you see?

On the surface, the top-line numbers look exhilarating. Revenue marched from ₹11 crore in FY22 to ₹38 crore in FY23, ₹51 crore in FY24, ₹72 crore in FY25, ₹80 crore in FY26, and crossed ₹111 crore trailing. Operating profits followed, rising to ₹24 crore in FY26 and ₹26 crore trailing. If you stopped your analysis right there, you would think you had discovered an extraordinary growth compounder.

Now look at the first forensic red flag: where did the profit actually come from? In FY25, Kody reported ₹24 crore in profit before tax, and other income was just ₹1 crore. That was clean. But in FY26, reported profit before tax was ₹26 crore, and ₹7 crore of that—more than a quarter of the entire pre-tax profit—came from 'other income'! In the trailing twelve months, other income reached ₹9 crore out of ₹29 crore in pre-tax profit. What is this other income? It is interest on unspent warrant proceeds, bank fixed deposit returns, and investment gains. When you strip that away, Kody's core operating profit from building robots and writing software has barely grown over the last eighteen months. Bottom-line stability was manufactured by treasury returns.

Now turn to the second red flag: where is the cash? In FY26, Kody reported ₹17 crore in net profit, but operating cash flow was only ₹12 crore. Why? Because customer receivables swallowed the rest. Debtor days rose from 103 days at the IPO to 163 days, then 177 days, and finally 192 days in FY26. Net working capital days exploded from 62 days to 197 days. In September 2026, out of total company assets of ₹298 crore, a staggering ₹177 crore—nearly 60% of everything Kody owns—was locked up in 'other assets', which is corporate jargon for uncollected customer invoices and unbilled project advances. Kody is essentially lending money to its customers so they can buy Kody's robots.

Now look at the capital expenditure. To build its assembly plant and manufacture demonstrator fleets, Kody spent ₹65 crore in cash capex in FY26 alone. Subtract ₹65 crore in capex from ₹12 crore in operating cash, and you arrive at a free cash flow deficit of negative ₹53 crore! Across FY25 and FY26 combined, Kody incinerated over ₹94 crore in free cash flow. How does a company with ₹17 crore in annual profit survive a ₹94 crore cash drain? It survives by issuing equity shares and convertible warrants to outside investors, which expanded balance sheet reserves from ₹66 crore to ₹215 crore and pushed promoter ownership down from 73% to below 69%.

This is the unvarnished forensic reality of Kody Technolab. The company is not compounding cash; it is consuming cash to establish a manufacturing and market footprint. There is nothing illegal or improper about this—many early-stage hardware pioneers go through a capital-absorption phase. But you and I must underwrite reality as it exists today, not as management wishes it to be. Kody is a conditional, capital-intensive industrial transformation, and until it proves it can collect its receivables and generate positive free cash flow, it cannot be classified as a compounder.

Let you and I take a deeper forensic look at the composition of Kody's balance sheet, because it reveals the true cost of this corporate expansion. Between March 2025 and September 2026, total balance sheet assets expanded from ₹112 crore to ₹298 crore. Where did all of that capital go? Look at the asset side of the ledger: fixed assets and capital work-in-progress grew from ₹15 crore to ₹86 crore as the company built out its Gandhinagar assembly plant and acquired specialized tooling. But the single largest line item on the balance sheet—standing at a staggering ₹177 crore in September 2026—is 'other assets'. That single line accounts for nearly 60% of everything Kody owns.

What does 'other assets' actually mean in forensic accounting terms? It consists of trade receivables, unbilled project milestones, capital advances to component vendors, and security deposits. In essence, nearly two-thirds of Kody's balance sheet consists of promises from customers and vendors, rather than cash in the bank or productive plant and machinery. In any manufacturing business, when trade receivables and unbilled assets grow significantly faster than top-line revenue, it is an unmistakable warning sign that commercial terms are being loosened to accelerate reported growth.

Now examine how this asset expansion was funded. It was not funded by retained earnings; cumulative free cash flow over the last two years was negative ₹94 crore. It was not funded by long-term bank borrowings; total borrowings stood at a modest ₹27 crore in September 2026. It was funded almost entirely by issuing equity shares and convertible warrants to outside strategic investors, which caused balance sheet reserves to swell from ₹66 crore to ₹215 crore. Management has essentially paid for its factory and financed its customer receivables by issuing new shares, steadily diluting existing owners. An investor who buys Kody today must ask: what happens when the warrant money runs out? If operating cash flow does not turn strongly positive, the company will have no choice but to tap the equity market again, further diluting per-share intrinsic value.

A final forensic test of earnings durability is to examine how much capital is required to generate each incremental rupee of revenue. In a scalable software business, the incremental capital requirement is near zero: once an application is coded, serving the thousandth customer costs almost nothing. In Kody's current hardware robotics operating model, the incremental capital requirement is intense. To grow revenue by ₹30 crore over the past two fiscal years, Kody had to invest over ₹110 crore in cash capital expenditures and expand its working capital by tens of crores. When an enterprise requires four rupees of capital to produce one rupee of new revenue, that is not an asset-light technology compounder; that is a capital-intensive manufacturing business that must earn an exceptional return on capital employed to justify its existence.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: When nearly 60% of a company's total balance sheet assets consist of uncollected receivables and working-capital advances, and free cash flow runs at negative ₹53 crore, headline accounting earnings are an illusion. The entire investment thesis hinges on whether those receivables convert into cash before the company needs another dilutive equity raise.
